title: Spinning a bamboo and silk blend
subtitle: A cool, lustrous plant-protein blend for summer garments
excerpt: Bamboo and silk both have high lustre and cool drape. Blended 70:30 bamboo-to-silk, they spin into a fine, smooth yarn with a silky handle and good stitch definition. The blend takes acid dye to a brilliant depth of colour.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from standard guild workshop practice for plant-protein fibre blends. Bamboo viscose and silk are commercially blended and sold as top in the handspinning trade; the spinning characteristics described here draw on standard guild guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: A spinning technique where fibres are combed parallel and drafted ahead of the twist, producing a smooth, strong yarn.
The natural sheen of a fibre. Both bamboo and silk have high lustre, giving the blend a distinctive sheen.
A fibre derived from an animal or plant protein source. Silk is a protein fibre; bamboo viscose is technically a regenerated cellulose fibre but is often grouped with protein fibres in handspinning.

attrs.title: Slippery fibre note
attrs.body: Bamboo and silk singles can back-slip through the wheel orifice. Check take-up tension before each spinning session.

items.name: Bamboo-silk blended top (70:30 bamboo:silk or similar)
Spinning wheel with a high ratio (14:1 to 18:1)

content.text: Draw the blended top into a pencil-thin rope before starting. Bamboo-silk top is slicker than wool top and can split into uneven strips if you draft from the main mass without predrafting first. A pre-drawn rope 10 to 15 cm in diameter gives a consistent supply at the wheel. Pull slowly and evenly; the fibres offer very little resistance and will over-draft in one quick pull.

Set a high drive ratio (14:1 to 18:1) and a firm take-up tension. Both bamboo and silk fibres need substantially more twist than wool to hold the singles together because the smooth fibre surface has no scale-interlocking to assist cohesion. If the singles separate or untwist when you stop treadling, the twist is too low. The take-up should be just firm enough to draw the singles onto the bobbin without pulling them apart.

Ply two singles together at a ratio slightly below the singles twist. Bamboo-silk 2-ply is balanced at a lower plying twist than wool because the individual fibres are long and the twist per inch is already high. Test by letting a short folded length of ply hang free: it should hang straight without coiling. Skein and wash in warm water (not hot; bamboo viscose can soften excessively in boiling water). Dry flat.

items.problem: The singles keep slipping back through the orifice
items.cause: Take-up tension is too loose for the weight of the singles accumulating on the bobbin
items.fix: Increase the take-up spring tension by half a step and re-spin. Check that the brake band is sitting correctly if using a Scotch-tension wheel.

items.problem: The yarn drafts in very uneven thick-thin sections
items.cause: The top was not predrafted and is drafting from the full mass, producing very thin sections alternating with undrafted lumps
items.fix: Predraft the top into a consistent rope before starting. Bamboo-silk top needs more preparation than wool top because the fibres lack the tactile feedback that tells you when the draft is uneven.
